cells.tense: You're in the middle of the exchange and you can see its shape.
cells.ask: Let one arrangement you've kept running end and clear up what's left over, so you can see what it makes room for.
cells.core:
This is the part of you that catches an imbalance in the middle of a conversation and says something early, before it turns into a debt. You can name what you gave and what came back without turning it into a score, and the people around you stop bracing for the moment you'll do the math.

The catch is that naming it first costs you the easy version of the moment — you get to be the one who noticed, which is not the same as being the one who's liked for it. Ending what's already finished asks something an open arrangement doesn't, and doing it can feel like you're the one who broke the deal. The room it clears is yours to stand in either way.

cells.tense: You're already counting the next round before the current one has happened.
cells.ask: Say your number once and then leave it alone for the whole day, letting whoever heard it sit with it.
cells.core:
On a working day here you settle things as they happen — you hand back what you borrowed, you take a correction without relitigating it, you let a small imbalance go because you can see it will even out. The books stay closed because the balance gets handled in real time.

What's running now is that fairness has become accounting. You know who came up short, who owes what, what the last one cost you — and a lot of it can't be said, so it keeps running in the background of every other conversation. The strain isn't the unfairness; it's holding the ledger open. Saying the number once and leaving it for the day gives your attention something to do that isn't running the figures again.

cells.tense: You're still standing where the trade turned, and you've been letting it stand since.
cells.ask: Name one thing that's genuinely owed to you to the person who owes it, then leave the answer with them for a day.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you ask for what's yours in a plain voice — a favor returned, a shift covered, a split where one side did more. You can hear a correction without needing the other person to agree first, and saying the thing doesn't require a whole case built behind it.

What's happening instead is you've stopped asking. Disproportion goes by unmentioned, you take more than your half of the work, and it passes for patience while the right to say anything has quietly gone quiet. A steady practice of your own feeds this — not by pushing feeling into the silence, but by giving your sense of what's fair something firm under it, so one true sentence doesn't need a court behind it.

cells.tense: The tally is running without you at the desk, and the entries are ones you'd never admit to writing.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been carrying without saying so, and either say it plainly to the person or put the whole account down openly, once.
cells.core:
On a working day your read on a situation lands before you can explain it — you know which way a thing is going to tip, and you act on it early enough that nothing piles up into a mood.

What's actually happening is the weighing goes on underneath your read of the room. You register who came up short, who got more than their share, and you don't connect that counting to anything you're doing — it just shows up as a slight distance or a low feeling you'd call something else. Bringing one entry up where you can see it, and putting it down out loud or on paper, gives the pattern something to end against instead of just accumulating.
